assessmentSummary.identity: Glute Bridge is a supine floor-supported bilateral bent-knee hip-extension cycle. With both feet supported, raise the hips through a comfortable active range, then lower and reset under control. This excludes Hip Thrust, bridge march, walkout, single-leg bridge, static hold, loaded floor bridge, testing, and forced range.
currentCardFindings: Source 64 lacks an exact cycle, range/support contract, load/fatigue tracking, alternate boundaries, calibration, and review gates.
Floor support distinguishes it from Hip Thrust; march, walkout, single-leg, hold, and loading materially change task structure.

proposedTaxonomy.intent: low-load active floor hip extension and control

assessmentSummary.programmingDecision: Candidate-only floor-supported bilateral Glute Bridge. Treat declared range, tempo, foot position, and brief pause as modifiers; assess Hip Thrust, march, walkout, single-leg, static, and loaded versions separately.

currentCardSnapshot.description: Lie supine with both knees bent and feet supported on the floor. Raise the hips through a comfortable active range, then lower and reset under control. One repetition is one bilateral floor-supported hip rise and return. This excludes Hip Thrust, bridge march, walkout, single-leg bridge, static hold, loaded floor bridge, testing, and forced end range.

environment.space: room to lie, bridge, and exit safely
environment.changeRule: Changing upper-body support, laterality, load, range, foot position, pause, tempo, dose, surface, or intent requires revalidation.

selectionPrerequisites: can use the supine floor base and exit safely
can perform a small bilateral active hip rise without symptom escalation
session logistics and downstream demands fit
excludeOrEscalate: symptom, restriction, unsafe supine base, surface, or communication conflict
sharp, increasing, unfamiliar, neurologic, circulation, breathing, chest, balance, or communication concern
notEstablishedByEvidence: universal foot position, hip height, dose, recovery, outcome, readiness threshold, or clinical clearance

claims: Glute Bridge is a supine floor-supported bilateral bent-knee hip-extension cycle: feet stay supported, hips rise through a comfortable active range, then return under control.
It excludes upper-back-supported Hip Thrust, bridge march, walkout, single-leg bridge, static hold, loaded floor bridge, diagnostic test, and forced end range.

evidence.sourceTitle: Electromyographic differences of the gluteus maximus, gluteus medius, biceps femoris, and vastus lateralis between the barbell hip thrust and barbell glute bridge
claims: Floor versus upper-back support changes exercise geometry and is a hard Hip Thrust/Glute Bridge boundary.
Tempo, pause, range, foot placement, and support are explicit delivery dimensions only when the bilateral floor-supported rise-and-return cycle is preserved.

evidence.sourceTitle: Supine Bridge Exercise: A Narrative Review of the Literature (Part I)
claims: Record gluteal, hamstring, trunk, foot, hip, knee, and spine roles as task mechanics without diagnosis or isolated-muscle claims.
Bridge research does not establish a universal foot position, pelvis endpoint, activation ranking, or clinical outcome.

evidence.sourceTitle: Supine Bridge Exercise: A Narrative Review of the Literature (Part I)
claims: A valid candidate repetition is controlled hip extension and return from a floor-supported supine base; excessive lumbar extension is not extra hip range.
Use a comfortable active range and reset rather than passive end-range loading.

evidence.sourceTitle: Youth Resistance Training: Updated Position Statement Paper From the NSCA
claims: Difficulty values describe exercise complexity and physical demand only, never athlete skill, proficiency, age, or classification.
The bilateral unloaded baseline is low-load but requires foot, pelvis, trunk, breathing, and return control; independent calibration remains required.

evidence.sourceTitle: Acute effects of muscle stretching on physical performance, range of motion, and injury incidence in healthy active individuals: a systematic review
claims: Acute exercise response depends on dose and context; no universal readiness or recovery outcome is claimed.
Track repetitions, range, tempo, foot position, pelvic/trunk compensation, hamstring symptoms, and downstream work.

evidence.sourceTitle: Youth Resistance Training: Updated Position Statement Paper From the NSCA
claims: Use a clear stable floor or mat, space to lie and exit, optional padding, and a clear stop signal.
Selection is a workout-input decision, not an exercise-card population label.

evidence.sourceTitle: Youth Resistance Training: Updated Position Statement Paper From the NSCA
claims: No source establishes a universal Glute Bridge dose or range. Use a low-dose quality-limited candidate prescription.
Stop before pain, persistent cramping, compensation, breath-holding, or inability to control the return.
Instructions must name the floor-supported setup, bilateral feet, active hip rise, trunk boundary, controlled lower, and reset.
Reduce range or use another reviewed task before forcing height or continuing through persistent cramping.

evidence.sourceTitle: Youth Resistance Training: Updated Position Statement Paper From the NSCA
claims: Appropriate instruction, surface, progression, and communication are safeguards.
Stop for sharp/increasing pain, neurologic/circulation/breathing/dizziness symptoms, unsafe surface, persistent cramp, or uncorrectable compensation.

evidence.sourceTitle: Acute effects of muscle stretching on physical performance, range of motion, and injury incidence in healthy active individuals: a systematic review
claims: Use Glute Bridge only when the exact floor-supported low-load hip-extension task fits the session; it does not promise treatment, injury prevention, or transfer.
Any changed support, laterality, load, range, pause, tempo, dose, or substitution reruns selection, logistics, duration, fatigue, and validation.
Athlete support should show foot setup, small active hip rise, quiet trunk, controlled lower, self-check, and stop prompt.
Captions, transcript, stills, audio description, exact media match, and quality remain human-review requirements.

evidence.sourceTitle: Youth Resistance Training: Updated Position Statement Paper From the NSCA
claims: Coach support should include surface and exit check, foot/knee/pelvis/trunk observation, range and fatigue log, and escalation for unresolved symptoms.
Do not diagnose glute inhibition or prescribe an adjacent bridge as an automatic substitute.

evidence.sourceTitle: Youth Resistance Training: Updated Position Statement Paper From the NSCA
claims: Candidate supports include mat/padding, reduced range, still cues, captions, transcript, audio description, and reviewed substitutions when supine floor work is inaccessible.
These supports do not establish individual readiness.

evidence.sourceTitle: Electromyographic differences of the gluteus maximus, gluteus medius, biceps femoris, and vastus lateralis between the barbell hip thrust and barbell glute bridge
claims: Hip Thrust is a separate upper-back-supported definition; march, walkout, single-leg, static hold, and load change cycle, laterality, leverage, or force demand and require explicit assessment.
Foot placement, range, tempo, and a brief pause can be delivery modifiers only under the fixed bilateral floor bridge contract.
Three inherited direct YouTube URLs are retained only as unverified candidates; no playback, exact-match, accessibility, quality, reviewer, or approval claim is made.

alternateAssessments.name: Glute Bridge with Brief Pause
alternateAssessments.rationale: A declared short pause changes cadence only when the bilateral floor rise-return remains intact.

alternateAssessments.name: Hip Thrust
alternateAssessments.rationale: Upper-back support changes geometry, setup, range, and mechanics.

alternateAssessments.name: Glute Bridge March
alternateAssessments.rationale: Alternating foot lift adds single-leg support and pelvic-control sequence.

alternateAssessments.name: Glute Bridge Walkout
alternateAssessments.rationale: Repeated heel travel changes knee angle, lever length, and repetition boundary.

alternateAssessments.name: Single-Leg Glute Bridge
alternateAssessments.rationale: Single-leg support changes laterality, loading, balance, and fatigue.

alternateAssessments.name: Glute Bridge Iso Hold
alternateAssessments.rationale: A hold has a different contraction mode and dose boundary.

alternateAssessments.name: Loaded Floor Glute Bridge
alternateAssessments.rationale: A declared floor-supported pelvic load changes physical demand and dosage while preserving support geometry.
